claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 contains residual porosity and microstructural inhomogeneity.
A liquid-phase precursor method can produce nanostructured ZrB2 powder.
The precursor-derived ZrB2 powder can be rapidly consolidated at approximately 1800 °C.
The proposed processing route produces nanoscale grains.
The proposed processing route improves interparticle bonding.
The proposed processing route yields a uniformly dense microstructure with low porosity.
The liquid precursor method promotes uniform nucleation of nanoscale ZrB2 particles.
Nanoscale ZrB2 particles enhance diffusion during sintering.
Nanoscale ZrB2 particles enhance particle rearrangement during sintering.
Enhanced diffusion and particle rearrangement permit lower-temperature densification.
Lower porosity reduces defect sites that can evolve into holes during prolonged liquid-plating exposure.
The precursor-derived ZrB2 will be pore-free.
The precursor-derived material will have phase purity similar to conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
The precursor-derived ZrB2 will have significantly lower porosity than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
The precursor-derived ZrB2 will retain greater mechanical integrity during prolonged liquid-plating exposure.
The precursor-derived ZrB2 will have a lower risk of hole formation and component failure during liquid-plating service.
Both processing routes can be compared using composition- and dimension-matched samples subjected to identical plating-bath exposure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the product as pore-free, whereas other fields only predict low or reduced porosity and explicitly state that the achievable degree of densification remains uncertain.
